articles.title: Europa obligará a marcar todo el contenido creado por inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
Europa ha comenzado a aplicar una regla que etiquetará el contenido generado por inteligencia artificial. La Comisión Europea anunció que a partir del 2 de agosto entrarán en vigor nuevas obligaciones de transparencia para sistemas de IA. La medida busca que cualquier usuario pueda distinguir con claridad qué contenido ha sido generado por una máquina.
De acuerdo con un comunicado de prensa, el avance de la IA generativa ha complicado diferenciar entre el contenido creado por personas y aquel que producen los sistemas automatizados. La Comisión Europea afirma que estas dificultades abren la puerta a la desinformación, manipulación masiva, fraude y suplantación de identidad, riesgos que antes eran mucho más limitados.
Debido a ello, Europa comenzó a aplicar un etiquetado para contenido sintético que forma parte del Reglamento de la IA. Bajo esta regla, las grandes tecnológicas tienen la obligación de diseñar sus sistemas para que cualquier persona sepa, de forma explícita, cuándo está interactuando con una inteligencia artificial y no con un humano. Esto incluye a los chatbots, agentes virtuales y avatares que puedan confundirse con interlocutores reales.
Sumado a esto, las empresas deberán añadir marcas legibles que permitan detectar contenido generado o manipulado artificialmente. Esta marca de agua ya está disponible en modelos como Gemini, Sora o MetaAI y es imperceptible para los humanos. El único modo de saber que una imagen, texto o video es IA se hace a través de una herramienta de identificación.
La Comisión señala que las empresas están obligadas a avisar a sus usuarios cuando estén expuestos a herramientas que reconozcan emociones o realicen categorización biométrica. También deberán etiquetar los deepfakes y marcar textos de interés público que no hayan pasado por revisión humana.
¿Cómo se etiquetará el contenido generado por IA?
Para cumplir con lo que marca el Artículo 50 del Reglamento de IA, la Comisión Europea desarrolló un conjunto de iconos estandarizados para señalar contenido generado por inteligencia artificial. El objetivo es que estas marcas sean reconocibles de un vistazo, como otros símbolos que vemos en el entorno digital.
| Icono | Cuándo usar | Ejemplos de casos de uso | 
|---|---|---|
|  | Cuando la IA estuvo involucrada en la creación de contenido falso profundo (imagen, audio, video) o texto publicado o cuando se implementa una etiqueta de texto personalizada o una segunda capa interactiva. | Vídeo falso profundo con la etiqueta de texto «voces generadas con» seguida del icono básico. | 
|  | Cuando todo el contenido falso profundo (imagen, audio, video) o texto es completamente generado por IA sin elementos creados por humanos o control editorial humano (aparte de incitar). | Videos falsos profundos completamente generados por IA con políticos o eventos ficticios. Música o arte totalmente compuesto por IA. Resúmenes de noticias generados por IA | 
|  | Cuando el contenido preexistente hecho por el hombre se modificó parcialmente con IA convirtiéndolo en una falsificación profunda o texto sobre asuntos de interés público. | Una cara en una fotografía auténtica se intercambia con una cara de un político que usa IA. Fotografías auténticas de un apartamento vacío se amueblan con IA. | 
El brazo ejecutivo de la UE también publicó una guía detallada dirigida a proveedores y desarrolladores para ayudarles a cumplir con estas obligaciones de transparencia. El documento explica cómo demostrar el cumplimiento normativo, incluyendo la adhesión a un código de buenas prácticas enfocado en el contenido generado por IA. Según la Comisión, las directrices se elaboraron con ayuda de los Estados miembros, la Oficina de IA y otros representantes del sector.
Multas de hasta 15 millones de euros a quienes no cumplan
La vigilancia del cumplimiento de estas reglas recaerá en varios organismos, según sea el caso. La supervisión general quedará a cargo de las autoridades nacionales de vigilancia del mercado, mientras que la Oficina de IA será responsable de vigilar los sistemas bajo su competencia directa. Por último, el Supervisor Europeo de Protección de Datos entrará en juego cuando las instituciones de la UE actúen como proveedoras o usuarias de estos sistemas.
Aquellas empresas que no cumplan con las reglas podrían enfrentar sanciones ejemplares. La Comisión Europea establece que quienes no respeten estas obligaciones se enfrentarán a multas de hasta 15 millones de euros o el 3% de su facturación global anual, cualquiera que resulte más alta. Para instituciones o agencias de la UE, las sanciones solo llegarán a los 750.000 euros.
El comunicado menciona que el objetivo de toda esta normativa es fomentar la confianza en el ecosistema informativo. La proliferación de fake news y montajes hace que muchas personas no sepan que están mirando un contenido generado por IA, lo cual podría tener consecuencias catastróficas.

articles.title: FOMO in the SOC: Where AI Platforms like Claude Actually Fit
articles.text:
AI is moving incredibly fast, and every security leader is feeling the pressure to keep up.
AI platforms like Claude, Codex and Cursor are already helping security teams write detections, investigate alerts, summarize incidents, and automate repetitive work. The conversation has evolved from whether AI belongs in the SOC, to where each type of AI delivers the most value.
With so many new AI products entering the market, it's easy to assume one tool can solve every problem. In reality, different types of AI are designed for different jobs.
Understanding that difference is what transforms AI FOMO into better security outcomes.
Join AI SOC: Where Claude belongs in the SOC
AI is changing security operations
The way security teams work is changing quickly.
Attackers are already using AI to generate phishing campaigns, automate malware development, and move faster than ever before. At the same time, defenders are using AI to triage alerts, create detection rules, automate reporting, and simply reduce manual work in general.
The opportunity is enormous.
The challenge is deciding where each type of AI fits into the SOC.
Two kinds of AI, two different jobs
The easiest way to think about modern security operations is as three layers.
At the bottom are your existing security tools such as your SIEM, EDR, cloud security, identity platforms, email security, and everything else generating alerts.
In the middle is an autonomous AI SOC. Its job is to investigate every alert automatically, correlate findings across tools, apply organizational context, and most importantly, determine which alerts actually require human attention.
At the top are AI platforms like Claude, Cursor, and Codex. These are where analysts, detection engineers, and incident responders collaborate with AI to solve problems, write detections, create reports, hunt for threats, and make decisions.
These layers are all complementary and necessary for a successful SOC.
Why AI platforms like Claude shouldn't investigate every alert
AI platforms are incredibly capable, but they're designed to help people.
An analyst can ask Claude to explain suspicious PowerShell activity, summarize an investigation, draft a Sigma rule, or translate a detection into another query language. Those are excellent uses of AI.
But investigating thousands of alerts every day is a different challenge.
That kind of work needs an autonomous system that runs continuously, integrates with security tools, remembers organizational context, and investigates alerts around the clock without waiting for a human prompt.
Trying to use an AI platform as a 24/7 SOC investigator is a bit like asking a brilliant consultant to answer every phone call in a busy call center. The consultant is extremely valuable, but only when they're focused on the work that benefits from their expertise.
The tokenomics problem
There's another reason AI platforms aren't designed to investigate every security alert: economics.
Every investigation starts with context. An AI model needs endpoint telemetry, process trees, authentication logs, email history, threat intelligence, previous investigations, detection rules, and organizational knowledge before it can make a good decision.
Every piece of that context consumes tokens.
That's perfectly reasonable when an analyst asks Claude to help investigate a handful of incidents each day.
It becomes a very different equation when a SOC receives thousands of alerts every day.
Imagine using a large language model to perform a fresh investigation for every alert. Even if each investigation were relatively small, the organization would still be paying for tens of thousands of AI conversations every day, most of which would conclude that the alert is benign. As alert volume grows, the cost grows with it.
Enter the autonomous AI SOC.
Instead of treating every alert as a brand-new conversation with a large language model, a good AI SOC combines deterministic workflows, forensic analysis, organizational memory, cached context, and selective AI reasoning. Large language models are used where they add value, not for every step of every investigation.
The result is an architecture that can investigate every alert continuously while keeping costs predictable.
Using Claude to investigate every alert is a bit like using a Formula 1 car to deliver packages. It's an incredible piece of engineering, but it was designed for speed, not high-volume logistics. Enterprise SOCs need infrastructure built to handle enormous scale efficiently, with AI applied where it has the greatest impact.
The MDR reality
There's another practical challenge that often gets overlooked.
Many organizations don't operate their own SOC. They rely on a MDR provider to monitor their environment.
In those environments, the MDR typically owns the investigation workflow. They have the analysts, the case management system, the investigation history, and often the enriched telemetry collected during the investigation. The customer usually receives only the escalated incidents and periodic reports, not every piece of evidence gathered along the way.
That makes it difficult for an AI platform like Claude to independently investigate alerts, because it doesn't have access to the same information the MDR is using.
Even if an organization wanted to build its own AI-assisted investigation workflow, it would first need the raw alerts, telemetry, investigation artifacts, and historical context that often remain inside the MDR's platform.
AI platforms are incredibly valuable once information is available to them, but they can't reason over data they don't have.
This is another reason autonomous AI SOC are becoming an important architectural layer. They sit directly alongside the organization's security tools, investigate alerts as they arrive, retain organizational context, and make that knowledge available to both analysts and AI platforms.
Instead of replacing MDRs overnight, they give organizations a path toward owning their investigations, their institutional knowledge, and ultimately their security operations.
Investigating 100% of alerts?
Most security teams simply don't have the capacity to investigate every alert they receive.
As a result, they prioritize the highest-severity alerts while lower-severity alerts often receive less attention.
The problem is that severity doesn't always reflect risk.
Analysis of more than 25 million security alerts processed during 2025 found that nearly 1% of confirmed incidents originated from low-severity or informational alerts. The conclusion is straightforward, meaningful threats can begin anywhere in the alert stream.
But the answer isn't asking analysts to work harder. It's giving them more capacity.
An autonomous AI SOC creates that capacity by investigating every alert, not just the loudest ones, while escalating only the cases that truly need human judgment.
Where Claude and friends shine
Once an autonomous AI SOC has completed the investigation, AI platforms become even more valuable.
Instead of spending time gathering evidence from multiple consoles, analysts can use an AI platform to focus on higher-value work.
They can:
- Ask questions about completed investigations.
- Draft and refine detection rules.
- Hunt for emerging threats.
- Summarize investigations for stakeholders.
- Generate incident reports.
- Explore new hypotheses.
- Make the final decisions on complex cases.
In other words, the autonomous AI SOC handles the grind of triaging endless alerts and repetitive investigation.
The AI platform helps people think, create, and decide based on everything the AI SOC has provided.
Better together
The biggest takeaway isn't that organizations need to choose between an autonomous AI SOC and AI platforms like Claude.
They need both.
One continuously investigates alerts across the environment.
The other helps security professionals work faster and make better decisions.
Together they create a model where machines handle repetitive investigation while humans focus on strategy, judgment, and continuous improvement.
Join Intezer's Co-Founder and CEO, Itai Tevet, and CMO Lital Asher-Dotan for a real conversation (not another stuffy webinar) about where AI actually fits in security operations today. With so many AI platforms competing for attention, Itai and Lital will cut through the noise and get specific about what to use where, based on real examples.
Three takeaways:
- Why AI platforms like Claude are built to help people, not investigate every alert at scale
- How the "tokenomics" of AI investigation change the math for high volume SOCs
- Where an autonomous AI SOC and AI platforms complement each other

articles.title: Por que astronautas da NASA estão treinando debaixo d'água para voltar à Lua?
articles.text:
Antes de explorar a Lua, os futuros astronautas do programa Artemis IV passaram por um treinamento debaixo d’água. Recentemente, os geólogos da NASA Trevor Graff e Angela Garcia participaram de uma simulação no Laboratório de Flutuabilidade Neutra (Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, NBL), no Centro Espacial Johnson, em Houston. A instalação abriga um enorme tanque usado para reproduzir parte das condições que os astronautas encontrarão durante as futuras missões ao satélite natural da Terra.
Mas por que esse tipo de treinamento é importante para a exploração lunar?
Para quem tem pressa:
- Geólogos da NASA participaram de um treinamento subaquático que simula parte das condições que os astronautas enfrentarão durante as futuras missões do programa Artemis à Lua;
- O enorme tanque do Laboratório de Flutuabilidade Neutra (NBL) foi adaptado para reproduzir características do polo sul lunar, permitindo testar ferramentas, equipamentos científicos e procedimentos de exploração;
- Os resultados dos testes ajudarão a preparar os astronautas para futuras missões tripuladas, com foco na coleta de amostras e na realização de pesquisas na superfície da Lua.
Como uma piscina ajuda a preparar missões espaciais?
Embora a água não reproduza exatamente a gravidade da Lua, ela permite criar um ambiente controlado para treinamentos e adaptação dos astronautas. Dentro do tanque, que possui cerca de 12 metros de profundidade, os tripulantes da missão podem praticar movimentos, testar equipamentos e aperfeiçoar procedimentos de segurança.
Para o treinamento do programa Artemis, parte da piscina foi transformada em um cenário semelhante ao da superfície lunar. O local recebeu solo e rochas que simulam o terreno da Lua, além da baixa iluminação para reproduzir as condições que os astronautas encontrarão no polo sul do satélite natural, um dos locais que a missão Artemis IV visa explorar.
Nesse ambiente, Graff e Garcia avaliaram ferramentas de geologia que poderão ser usadas durante futuras missões tripuladas, além de realizar testes de instalação de equipamentos científicos.
Leia mais:
- Artemis 3: NASA começa a montar foguete da missão
- Artemis 3 será a missão mais complexa da NASA desde a era Apollo
- Tremores lunares podem revelar gelo enterrado nas crateras do polo sul da Lua
Segundo a NASA, esta foi a primeira vez que dois geólogos participaram simultaneamente de um treinamento de geologia lunar no NBL como parte do programa Artemis.
Os resultados dos testes serão usados para auxiliar no treinamento dos astronautas que participarão das próximas missões com pouso na Lua. O objetivo é garantir que as equipes estejam preparadas para realizar a coleta de amostras e operar equipamentos em uma das regiões mais desafiadoras do satélite natural.
Layse Ventura é editora de SEO no Olhar Digital e mestre pela UFSC.

articles.title: Alles nur Hype? So wenige durch KI aufgedeckte Schwachstellen wurden tatsächlich aktiv ausgenutzt
articles.text:
Sicherheitsexperten zeigen: Nur ein Prozent der durch KI aufgedeckten Schwachstellen wurde wirklich ausgenutzt
Zahlreiche Verantwortliche von diversen Diensten, Webseiten und Anwendungen kämpfen aktuell mit demselben Problem. Durch KI-Tools, die Sicherheitslücken in ihren Werken in kürzester Zeit aufspüren können, werden sie mit Sicherheitsberichten überschwemmt. Das hat jetzt schon dazu geführt, dass unter anderem GitHub Änderungen am Bug-Bounty-Programm durchgeführt hat. Eine Untersuchung von Vuln Check zeigt indes, dass nur wenige der per KI aufgespürten Lücken wirklich zur aktiven Gefahr geworden sind.
So viele aktive Sicherheitslücken konnte KI aufspüren
Als Grundlage hat Vuln Check dafür zwei Datensets herangezogen. Zunächst analysierten die Sicherheitsforscher:innen Cybersecurity-Meldungen, bei denen Anthropics KI als Mitwirkende genannt wird. Die Daten gehen dabei bis zum April 2026 zurück, als Anthropic Project Glasswing angekündigt hatte. Dazu kommen Daten der Berkeley Vulnerability Research Initiative, die ebenfalls KI-gestützte Sicherheitsmeldungen aufzeichnet.
Insgesamt konnten die Sicherheitsforscher:innen so auf Daten von 1.061 KI-Meldungen zurückgreifen. Im Anschluss haben sie untersucht, ob es Anzeichen dafür gibt, dass die Lücken aktiv ausgenutzt wurden. Das Ergebnis: Nur 14 der über 1.000 gemeldeten Lücken wurden schon von Hacker:innen ausgenutzt. Alle anderen sind zwar echte Lücken in den Systemen, aber wurden weder von Angreifer:innen noch von Verteidiger:innen vorab gefunden.
Die Sicherheitsforscher:innen schreiben dazu, dass mit KI gefundene Sicherheitslücken zwar Wert für Angreifer:innen und Verteidiger:innen haben, aber die Daten nicht darauf hindeuten, dass die Schwachstellen häufiger als solche ausgenutzt werden, die händisch aufgespürt wurden. Sie ergänzen: „KI scheint die Anzahl der Schwachstellen, die entdeckt werden können, so zu erhöhen, dass Verteidiger:innen die Möglichkeit haben, sie zu identifizieren und zu schließen, bevor Angreifer:innen damit etwas machen können.“
Dennoch ist der Zeitraum, bis veröffentlichte Sicherheitslücken ausgenutzt werden, deutlich geschrumpft. Lag er 2025 noch bei 120 Tagen nach der Bekanntmachung einer Schwachstelle, sind es in der ersten Jahreshälfte 2026 lediglich noch 80 Tage. Sicherheitslücken werden also nicht schneller ausgenutzt, bevor sie bekannt werden, aber nach der Veröffentlichung schneller von Angreifer:innen rekonstruiert und gegen ungeschützte Dienste und Geräte eingesetzt.
Abschließend schreibt Vuln Check dazu: „Aktuell bekommen Verteidiger:innen durch den Zugang zu fortschrittlichen KI-Modellen eher einen Vorteil durch das Stärken ihrer Software, als Angreifer:innen darin, Sicherheitslücken vor den Softwareproduzent:innen zu finden. […] Das bedeutet aber nicht, dass das Risiko imaginär wäre. Es bedeutet, dass die echten Auswirkungen noch moderat sind und es trotzdem wichtig ist, ein genaues Auge darauf zu behalten, wie sich die Technologie entwickelt, als nur auf den Hype zu reagieren.“

articles.title: Your Fitbit data can now connect directly to Apple Health
articles.text:
Google is rolling out an update that will finally allow you to connect your Fitbit workouts, steps, vitals, and other data to Apple Health, as reported earlier by 9to5Mac. With Google Health’s 5.05 update, you can now tap your profile icon, select “Partner apps,” and choose Apple Health to link your data directly.
Your Fitbit data can now connect directly to Apple Health
Google Health can sync your workouts, steps, and vitals to Apple Health.
Previously, you could only import your Apple Health data into Google Health, but not the other way around. That meant using third-party apps — like Power Sync for Fitbit or Fitbit to Apple Health Sync — or some other kind of workaround to connect your Google Health information to Apple Health.
Google Health replaced the Fitbit app in May. The new app had a bit of a rocky rollout after users raised concerns over the new AI health coach, user interface, and other issues, though Google has since addressed some of these complaints.
Along with this update, Google announced that users in the US can use Smart Health Links to share medical records with a provider or family member. You can create a link by heading to the Health tab, choosing the “Medical” section, selecting “Shareable records,” and tapping the “plus” icon. From there, you can choose which data you want to include in the link and share it via a URL or QR code.

articles.title: Wispr Flow is preparing to launch a meeting notetaker, updated terms suggest | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Dictation app Wispr Flow is preparing to launch a meeting notetaker, according to the tool’s updated Terms of Service.
The company also sent an email to its customers about the change in both its terms and its privacy policy to accommodate related features.
Upon investigation, the refreshed terms have added sections about the use of meeting data and the notetaker. The company said the notetaker will generate transcripts, summaries, actions, and insights, writing:
For Notetaker, Input may also include Meeting Data, including meeting audio, participant information, meeting metadata, speaker labels, meeting transcripts, and other information processed in connection with a meeting. Output may include AI-generated meeting transcripts, summaries, action items, meeting insights, speaker attribution, and other meeting-related content.
With the launch, the startup will take on other meeting notetakers such as Granola, Fireflies, Read AI, Otter, and Fathom. Wispr Flow’s co-founder Tanay Kothari had previously talked about building an AI assistant in interviews. With a meeting notetaker, Wispr Flow would gain additional context about its users and could automate more tasks beyond cleaning up spoken sentences.
It’s not clear if the startup wants to launch a Granola-style notetaker that relies on system audio and transcribes the meeting without keeping a recording, or build a full-fledged meeting recording tool.
To date, Wispr Flow has raised more than $81 million, with the company valued at $700 million at its last round. In May, Bloomberg reported that the company was in talks for a new round, valuing it at $2 billion.
Wispr Flow didn’t respond to our request for further comment.

articles.title: From Blueprint To Build: Engineering The World's Largest AI Chips
articles.text:
Building hyper-large form factor packages that measure up to 240 mm x 240 mm with reliable encapsulation.
By Sujit Sharan and Yang Guo
Today’s most advanced AI systems rely on larger, more complex assemblies of dies and chiplets from multiple process nodes and foundries, driving unprecedented demands on advanced packaging. At the 2026 IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC), two Intel Foundry research teams presented complementary approaches to meet this shift: one outlined an architectural blueprint for the next generation of AI chip packages, while the other tackled a key manufacturing constraint that emerges as those packages expand. For customers building AI platforms, these advances point to higher compute density per system, better energy efficiency, and the ability to scale next-generation workloads without completely new system architectures.
Our Advanced Design team described how to design and build hyper-large form factor (HLFF) packages measuring up to 240 mm x 240 mm, integrating arrays of compute dies with high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and I/O components on a single platform. In parallel, the Assembly Technology Development team developed material and process innovations to enable reliable encapsulation at these larger scales. Together, these efforts help move HLFF packaging from concept toward manufacturable reality, supporting AI data centers, scientific supercomputing, and large-scale model training systems.
For decades, computing performance improved by shrinking transistors. As the demand for compute accelerates and more components are needed in a single package, process node scaling is increasingly enhanced by integrating more silicon at the package level by assembling multiple chips into a cohesive system.
Our Advanced Design team extends this approach to an unprecedented scale with HLFF packages. These designs integrate arrays of compute dies with HBM and I/O components, connected by Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge-T (EMIB-T) technology. These embedded silicon bridges provide high-density interconnects, enabling data transfer rates above 64 gigabits per second (Gb/s) per channel.¹ For system designers, this means greater compute density and lower latency than multi-package approaches.
The research explores two configurations. Configuration A uses EMIB-T bridges for all chip-to-chip communication, maximizing bandwidth and yield recovery. Configuration B routes processor communication through the substrate, reducing hardware complexity while trading off some performance. Each offers a different balance of performance, cost, and design flexibility.
Both approaches scale toward packages as large as 240 mm x 240 mm, with a roadmap extending beyond 12x reticle integration and toward panel-scale systems approaching 50x further out.¹ Together, they define a path to building the largest and most complex AI compute platforms to date.
Fig. 1: Schematic depicting the progressive scaling of packages from 8x reticle size within the standard 120 mm x 120 mm footprint up to the 240 mm x 240 mm HLFF.
Moving from today’s packages to HLFF scale means solving several linked engineering problems at once.
Moving data fast enough. Inside the package, EMIB-T bridges with metal layers finer than 2 micrometers (µm) enable the 64 Gb/s per channel speeds AI workloads require for chip-to-chip and chip-to-memory connections. For communication leaving the package, the research evaluates co-packaged copper cable connectors and co-packaged optics as the leading approaches for reaching the industry’s projected next off-package speed target of 448 Gb/s.¹
Delivering power efficiently. Routing power from the package edges becomes increasingly inefficient at HLFF scale. The research proposes embedding silicon capacitors within the substrate and directly beneath the chips, providing up to 1 millifarad (mF) of local energy storage per full reticle chip area.¹ Moving voltage regulators onto or into the package also lets them respond faster to changing chip power demands.
Building redundancy for yield. The team proposes adding spare communication lanes alongside active ones. Adding just three to four spare lanes to every group of 64 raises bundle yield from about 97% to above 99%.¹ At HLFF scale, this difference is key to making products economically manufacturable.
Keeping the package flat. The research team modeled free-standing warpage of up to 7 mm at room temperature, enough to disrupt electrical connections and thermal contact. The proposed solution combines thick stiffener rings, low-expansion glass-core substrates, and a multi-ball solder ball process. During operation, pressing the cooling hardware down with force above approximately 4,500 newtons (N) helps keep the package nearly flat.
Managing heat at kilowatt scale. HLFF packages are expected to operate at 15 to 25 kilowatts (kW) total, with localized hot spots that demand aggressive cooling. Instead of one large cold plate, the research proposes a modular, cell-based cooling architecture with independently controlled thermal zones and embedded sensors, designed to scale beyond 5 kW of cooling per module.
One challenge the blueprint flags but does not fully solve is encapsulation: sealing the chips onto the package with a protective material. As packages grow, that process becomes much harder. That is where the Assembly Technology Development team’s work comes in.
Chip encapsulation relies on an underfill material that flows underneath the chip by capillary action and protects the joints between the chips and the substrate. This works well at smaller scales. But as packages and chip sizes grow, the material has to travel larger distances, making it more challenging to achieve a complete fill.
The scaling impact is clear: earlier packages required maximum underfill flow distances of about 22 mm. Today’s large EMIB packages exceed 43 mm flow distance. At the 5x to 10x reticle scales targeted by HLFF architectures, the flow distances grow even further and flow challenges become even more complex. Variations in chip surface materials and changes in joint pitch add more resistance, making uniform flow harder to achieve. Removing air pockets, or voids, reduces failure points and improves product reliability over its operational lifetime.
Fig. 2: Demonstration of underfill flow distance across three generations of package designs: (a) 22.5 mm, (b) 28.5 mm, and (c) 43.8 mm.
Our Assembly Technology Development team addressed encapsulation through three coordinated levers: material, dispense strategy, and cure.
First, the underfill material was optimized to balance flow and reliability. Lower viscosity enables longer flow distances, but reducing filler content can increase thermal stress. The team developed a direct flow test on representative package vehicles to identify formulations that extend flow without sacrificing mechanical integrity.
Second, the dispensing strategy was redesigned. Instead of relying solely on edge dispensing, the team introduced multi-point application, including between dies, to reduce effective flow distances and improve coverage.
Finally, the cure process was tuned to eliminate defects after dispense. Optimized cure conditions collapsed voids, turning packages with defects up to 3.4 mm into fully void-free results.² Together, these advances reduce defect risk and improve process consistency at larger scales.
Fig. 3: Comparison of the same package under two cure conditions. Image (a) shows voids with equivalent diameters up to 3.4 mm. Image (b) shows a completely void-free result achieved with an optimized cure condition.
These innovations were validated across package types aligned with HLFF architectures. An EMIB-based package exceeding 5x reticle, with 18 dies including 12 HBM stacks, achieved void-free encapsulation at flow distances above 40 mm. Larger tiled EMIB packages beyond 7x reticle also showed void-free results. In Foveros 3D packages, void-free encapsulation was achieved at 2x and 4x reticle scales, with the 2x design passing full reliability testing, including 700 temperature cycles and over 1,000 hours of high-temperature stress testing.²
While scaling to full HLFF dimensions remains a future step, this work establishes critical process capability by linking architectural vision with manufacturable building blocks.
The work presented at ECTC 2026 advances encapsulation to 7x reticle scales and defines architectures up to 240 mm x 240 mm, but both teams are already pushing further. The roadmap targets packages beyond 12x reticle in the near term and panel-scale systems approaching 50x, enabled by continued pitch scaling, active bridge integration, and co-packaged optics. Encapsulation research is advancing toward those same scales, aligning manufacturing capability with architectural ambition.
These developments provide customers a clear path to scale future AI systems with higher compute density, new interconnect technologies, and next-generation deployment models.
Yang Guo is a packaging R&D engineer at Intel Foundry.
Engineers in Intel Foundry’s Advanced Design team contributed to the hyper-large form factor architecture research, including Sujit Sharan, Mohit Khurana, Aditya Vaidya, Kemal Aygun, Kaladhar Radhakrishnan, Jianyong Xie, Chinmay Potdar, Patrick Nardi, Sachin Deshmukh, Brandon Marin, Prasanna Raghavan, Satish Surana, Shripad Gokhale, and Nisha Ananthakrishnan. Engineers in Intel Foundry’s Assembly Technology Development team contributed to the encapsulation process research, including Yang Guo, Ziyin Lin, John C. Decker, James Breyfogle, Eylul Simsek, Hsin-yu Li, Yiqun Bai, Chengzi Huang, and Wen Yang.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Nigerian e-health startup NduLink joins FasterCapital’s EquityPilot programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian e-health startup NduLink has joined FasterCapital’s EquityPilot programme to accelerate go-to-market readiness for its MVP and initial city launches.
Founded by Stanley Anayochukwu, NduLink is building a localised, scalable infrastructure to improve access to verified providers and to coordinate care across hospitals, labs, and pharmacies.
It has now been selected for the EquityPilot programme run by FasterCapital, a global venture builder and online incubator dedicated to co-funding and co-founding innovative startups, which will focus in the first 30–60 days on product refinement, provider recruitment, and go-to-market readiness for NduLink’s MVP and initial city launches.
This support aims to move the startup from prototype to active provider onboarding without promising funding outcomes.
“We’re excited to support NduLink through EquityPilot. Our team will focus on execution milestones and connecting the startup with the right ecosystem stakeholders,” said Hesham Zreik, founder and CEO of FasterCapital.

articles.title: Managed IT And IT Outsourcing For Streamlined Daily Workflows - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Introduction to Managed IT and IT Outsourcing
In today’s fast-paced and technology-driven business environment, organizations are continually searching for ways to enhance operational efficiency, reduce costs, and maintain a competitive edge. One of the most effective strategies to achieve these goals is through managed IT services and IT outsourcing. These approaches allow businesses to delegate their IT management and support functions to specialized external providers, enabling them to streamline daily workflows, improve productivity, and focus more on their core business functions.
Managed IT and outsourcing services have become increasingly critical as companies face the challenges of rapidly evolving technology, cybersecurity threats, and the growing complexity of IT infrastructure. By partnering with expert providers, businesses gain access to advanced technology, proactive support, and scalable resources without the need to build and maintain large in-house IT departments. This shift not only reduces overhead costs but also increases agility, helping organizations respond swiftly to market changes and customer demands.
According to a recent report by Grand View Research, the global IT outsourcing market size was valued at USD 333.7 billion in 2021 and is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.4% from 2022 to 2030. This growth underscores the rising adoption of outsourcing as a strategic business practice.
The Value Proposition of Managed IT Services
Managed IT services represent a proactive approach to IT management, where external providers take responsibility for the oversight, maintenance, and optimization of an organization’s IT systems. This model ensures that IT infrastructure remains secure, updated, and efficient, minimizing the risk of downtime and costly disruptions.
One of the key advantages of managed IT services is their ability to offer continuous monitoring and rapid response to potential issues before they escalate. Automated tools used by managed service providers (MSPs) handle routine tasks such as patch management, system backups, and network monitoring, freeing internal staff from repetitive duties and reducing human error.
A report by MarketsandMarkets projects that the global managed services market size will grow from USD 223 billion in 2021 to USD 329 billion by 2026, reflecting widespread recognition of its benefits among businesses aiming to optimize IT operations.
A notable example in this space is ANC Group in the IT sector, a leader known for delivering tailored IT solutions that support businesses in maintaining seamless workflows. Their expertise allows clients to align their IT infrastructure with evolving business needs, ensuring agility and operational continuity. With services ranging from cybersecurity to cloud management, they offer comprehensive support that helps organizations stay ahead of technological trends and compliance requirements.
IT Outsourcing: A Strategic Advantage
Complementing managed services, IT outsourcing enables companies to delegate specific IT functions or entire operations to external experts. This approach provides several strategic benefits, including cost savings, access to specialized skills, and the ability to scale resources flexibly.
Outsourcing IT allows companies to convert fixed IT costs into variable expenses, paying only for the services they need when they need them. This financial flexibility is particularly valuable for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that may not have the budget to maintain extensive IT teams or infrastructure.
Further, outsourcing partners often bring niche expertise in areas such as cybersecurity, cloud computing, or software development, which may be difficult or expensive to cultivate internally. This access to advanced capabilities enables businesses to implement cutting-edge technologies and best practices without the learning curve or recruitment challenges.
A survey conducted by Deloitte found that 70% of businesses that outsource IT functions report improved service quality and cost efficiency, highlighting the tangible benefits of this approach.
For companies operating in competitive urban markets, collaborating with firms like APC Integrated for Boston businesses can provide customized IT outsourcing services tailored to local business environments. These partnerships help streamline workflows by managing routine IT maintenance, help desk support, and infrastructure administration, freeing internal teams to focus on strategic projects and innovation.
How Managed IT and Outsourcing Streamline Daily Workflows
The integration of managed IT services and outsourcing into business operations plays a pivotal role in streamlining daily workflows. This is achieved through several mechanisms:
– Automation of Routine Tasks: Managed service providers employ automation tools to handle patch management, system updates, backups, and network monitoring. Automating these repetitive tasks reduces manual errors and ensures consistent maintenance without burdening internal staff.
– Enhanced Network Reliability: Continuous monitoring and rapid incident response reduce downtime, ensuring that critical business applications remain available. Reliable IT infrastructure supports uninterrupted workflows and improves overall productivity.
– Improved Security Posture: Proactive threat detection, vulnerability assessments, and compliance management protect sensitive data and minimize the risk of cyberattacks. This security focus safeguards business continuity and customer trust.
– Scalable IT Resources: Outsourcing allows companies to adjust their IT capacity quickly in response to changing business demands, such as seasonal spikes or rapid growth, without the delays and capital expenditure associated with hiring and infrastructure expansion.
A recent IDC report revealed that organizations utilizing managed IT services experienced a 25% increase in operational efficiency within the first year of adoption. This efficiency translated into faster project completion, reduced downtime, and higher employee satisfaction.
Additionally, a report by CompTIA found that 59% of companies using managed services observed measurable improvements in end-user productivity due to enhanced IT support and reduced system disruptions.
Best Practices for Selecting Managed IT and Outsourcing Partners
Selecting the right managed IT or outsourcing provider is crucial to realizing the full benefits of these services. Businesses should carefully evaluate potential partners based on several criteria:
– Industry Expertise: Providers with experience in your industry will better understand the specific challenges and regulatory requirements you face.
– Service Level Agreements (SLAs): Clearly defined SLAs with measurable performance indicators ensure accountability and provide benchmarks for service quality.
– Technology Compatibility: Ensure the provider’s technology stack integrates seamlessly with your existing systems to avoid disruptions and facilitate smooth workflows.
– Flexibility and Scalability: Providers should offer customizable services that can evolve with your business needs, accommodating growth or changes in strategy.
– Proven Track Record: Look for client testimonials, case studies, certifications, and industry recognition that demonstrate the provider’s reliability and expertise.
Engaging with established firms offers the advantage of proven methodologies and extensive experience, which are invaluable for smooth onboarding and ongoing support. Their experience helps mitigate risks associated with IT transitions and ensures continuity during periods of change.
Similarly, partnering provides specialized knowledge of local market dynamics and customized IT outsourcing solutions, helping organizations optimize operations and focus on innovation.
Overcoming Challenges in IT Outsourcing and Managed Services
Despite their advantages, managed IT and outsourcing arrangements can present challenges, including communication gaps, data security concerns, and perceived loss of control.
To overcome these issues, organizations should:
– Establish Clear Communication Protocols: Regular meetings, transparent reporting, and defined escalation paths foster effective collaboration between internal teams and external providers.
– Implement Robust Data Protection Measures: Contracts should include clauses ensuring compliance with data privacy regulations such as GDPR or HIPAA, and providers should demonstrate strong security controls.
– Maintain Internal Liaison Teams: Designating internal staff to coordinate with providers helps preserve organizational knowledge and facilitates quick resolution of issues.
By proactively addressing these factors, companies can build strong, trust-based partnerships that deliver continuous improvement and align IT services with business goals.
Conclusion
Managed IT services and IT outsourcing have become indispensable strategies for businesses seeking to streamline daily workflows and enhance operational agility. By leveraging specialized expertise, advanced technologies, and scalable resources, organizations can reduce operational burdens, improve system reliability, and focus on strategic growth initiatives.
For companies looking to maximize these benefits, partnering with reputable providers offers a pathway to transform IT from a cost center into a strategic asset. Similarly, collaborating with
exemplifies how expert service providers can tailor solutions to meet evolving business needs, ensuring seamless workflows and sustained competitive advantage.
In an increasingly digital world, embracing managed IT and outsourcing is not merely an option but a strategic imperative. Organizations that adopt these approaches position themselves to thrive amid technological change, operational complexity, and market pressures-turning IT into a driver of innovation and efficiency.

articles.title: Cette tablette Xiaomi qui veut faire trembler l'iPad tombe sous les 400 € sur Amazon
articles.text:
Pour ceux qui cherchent une tablette premium sans passer par l'écosystème Apple, Xiaomi a présenté sa Pad 8 au MWC 2026 avec l'ambition claire de jouer dans la cour des grands. Ce modèle profite justement d'une remise importante sur Amazon : 389,30 € au lieu de 551 € en version 256 Go.
La Xiaomi Pad 8 embarque une dalle LCD de 11,2 pouces au format 3:2, avec une définition 3,2K (3200 x 2136 pixels) et un taux de rafraîchissement variable pouvant atteindre 144 Hz. Elle repose sur le processeur Qualcomm Snapdragon 8s Gen 4, gravé en 4 nm, avec un cœur Cortex-X4 cadencé jusqu'à 3,21 GHz, épaulé selon les configurations par 8 ou 12 Go de RAM. Sa batterie de 9200 mAh profite d'une charge rapide filaire de 45 W, dans un châssis tout métal unibody de seulement 5,75 mm d'épaisseur pour 485-486 g.
XIAOMI Pad 8 256 Go à 389,30 € au lieu de 551 € sur Amazon
Pourquoi choisir cette XIAOMI Pad 8 256 Go ?
- Un écran 144 Hz qui se ressent réellement à l'usage, un argument rare sur une tablette à ce niveau de prix
- Une puce Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 qui n'a pas à rougir face à des modèles nettement plus onéreux
- Un châssis tout métal unibody, pour une finition qui tranche avec l'entrée de gamme habituelle
Une tablette pensée pour concurrencer les modèles plus chers
Plusieurs tests soulignent que cette Pad 8 n'a "pas besoin de se cacher de la classe supérieure", grâce à un processeur rapide, une prise en charge native du stylet et un écran lumineux. La densité de pixels de 336 à 344 PPI selon les sources offre un rendu net et précis, comparable à ce que proposent des tablettes bien plus onéreuses. Un testeur va jusqu'à la qualifier de "meilleure alternative à l'iPad" pour un usage orienté divertissement et productivité, notamment grâce à son mode bureau compatible avec clavier et souris.
Un positionnement clairement tourné vers la productivité
Xiaomi mise beaucoup sur l'intégration native de fonctions IA et sur un mode bureau permettant d'associer clavier et stylet, pour transformer la tablette en outil de travail mobile. Un test évoque d'ailleurs la promesse de "remplacer votre ordinateur portable tout en tenant dans votre sac", une ambition qui reste à nuancer selon l'usage visé, mais qui illustre bien le positionnement voulu par la marque. La caméra principale de 13 Mpx reste correcte sans être un argument majeur, cette tablette misant surtout sur l'écran, la puissance et l'autonomie plutôt que sur la photographie.
✅ Les points forts
- Écran 3,2K à 144 Hz, une fréquence rare sur une tablette Android à ce tarif
- Processeur Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 performant, salué par plusieurs tests indépendants
- Châssis tout métal unibody fin (5,75 mm) et léger (485 g)
❌ Les limites
- Caméra principale de 13 Mpx correcte mais sans réelle avancée technologique
- Ambition de "remplacer un PC portable" à nuancer selon l'usage professionnel visé
- Version testée à 8 Go de RAM sur cette configuration, une capacité que d'autres tablettes premium dépassent déjà
XIAOMI Pad 8 256 Go à 389,30 € au lieu de 551 € sur Amazon
À 389,30 €, la Xiaomi Pad 8 256 Go devient une option difficile à ignorer pour qui cherche un écran haut de gamme, un processeur performant et une autonomie solide sans passer par le tarif habituel d'un iPad. Une remise qui renforce encore l'argument du rapport qualité-prix déjà mis en avant par la plupart des tests depuis son lancement.

articles.title: 7 Books that make you realise you can't control everything
articles.text:
7 Books that make you realise you can't control everything
Discover seven insightful books that explore uncertainty, acceptance, and the freedom that comes from letting go of control.
Many of us spend a surprising amount of time trying to control life. We plan every detail, worry about future outcomes, replay past mistakes, and attempt to manage how others think, feel, or behave. Yet despite our best efforts, life remains unpredictable. People change. Plans fall apart. Opportunities appear unexpectedly. Challenges arrive without warning.
The more we try to control every outcome, the more frustrated and anxious we often become. Some of the most powerful books on personal growth, philosophy, and psychology remind us of a difficult but liberating truth: we cannot control everything. What we can control is how we respond.
7 books that explore the wisdom of letting go
1. The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck by Mark Manson
Many struggles come from trying to control things that were never meant to be controlled. Mark Manson challenges the idea that a perfect life comes from avoiding problems or constantly chasing approval. Instead, he explains that peace comes from accepting difficulties, choosing what truly matters, and letting go of the things outside our influence.
The book teaches readers that they cannot control every outcome, other people's opinions, or every challenge they face. What they can control is how they respond and where they choose to direct their energy. For anyone learning to accept uncertainty and stop fighting against reality, The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fck* offers a practical perspective on focusing only on what truly matters.
2. The Wisdom of Insecurity by Alan Watts
Alan Watts argues that much of human anxiety comes from our desire for certainty. We want guarantees about careers, relationships, health, and the future. But life offers very few guarantees. Watts suggests that attempting to eliminate uncertainty only increases stress because uncertainty is woven into existence itself. The book encourages readers to embrace the present moment rather than constantly seeking control over what comes next. Its message is both challenging and deeply freeing.
3. When Things Fall Apart by Pema Chödrön
Life inevitably includes disappointment, loss, and unexpected change. In this compassionate and insightful book, Pema Chödrön explores what happens when our carefully constructed plans collapse. Instead of resisting uncertainty, she encourages readers to remain open to it.
The book teaches that suffering often increases when we insist that reality conform to our expectations. Acceptance, on the other hand, allows us to move through difficulties with greater resilience and wisdom.
4. The Black Swan by Nassim Nicholas Taleb
Many people believe the world is more predictable than it actually is. Taleb explores how rare and unexpected events, what he calls "Black Swans", often have enormous consequences. These events frequently shape history, careers, economies, and personal lives in ways that no one could have predicted.
The book challenges the illusion of control and highlights the limits of forecasting and planning. Readers come away with a deeper appreciation for uncertainty and adaptability.
5. Man's Search for Meaning by Viktor E. Frankl
Frankl's experiences in Nazi concentration camps led him to a profound realisation about control.
Even when nearly every external freedom had been taken away, individuals retained the ability to choose their attitude and response. This insight became the foundation of his philosophy.
The book demonstrates that while circumstances may be beyond our control, meaning and dignity can still be found through our choices. It remains one of the most powerful explorations of human resilience ever written.
6. The Book of Joy by the Dalai Lama and Desmond Tutu
Through conversations about happiness, suffering, and human experience, the Dalai Lama and Desmond Tutu repeatedly return to the theme of acceptance. The book acknowledges that pain, uncertainty, and disappointment are unavoidable parts of life.
Rather than trying to control every circumstance, the authors encourage cultivating gratitude, compassion, and perspective. Their approach offers a more sustainable path to peace than the endless pursuit of control.
7. Everything Is F*cked: A Book About Hope by Mark Manson
In this philosophical and often provocative book, Mark Manson examines humanity's desire for certainty, control, and predictability. He argues that many people struggle because they expect life to be controllable and fair. When reality fails to meet those expectations, frustration follows.
The book encourages readers to focus less on controlling outcomes and more on developing values, resilience, and perspective. Its message aligns with a timeless truth: life is unpredictable, but our response to it matters enormously.
What stays with us
Letting go of control can feel uncomfortable because it requires accepting that some questions will remain unanswered and some outcomes will remain uncertain. Yet it can also be incredibly liberating. Whether it's the Stoic wisdom of Meditations, the philosophical insights of The Wisdom of Insecurity, the compassionate guidance of When Things Fall Apart, the unpredictability explored in The Black Swan, the resilience of Man's Search for Meaning, the perspective of The Book of Joy, or the modern reflections of Everything Is Fcked*, these books remind us of an important truth: You do not need to control everything to live a meaningful life.
Sometimes peace begins when you stop fighting uncertainty and start learning how to live alongside it.

articles.title: New DOUBLECUP ClickFix service hides malware in browser cache images
articles.text:
A new Russian loader-as-a-service named DOUBLECUP uses ClickFix attacks to hide malicious code in PNG images cached by victims' browsers, ultimately delivering CountLoader to Windows and macOS devices and a new remote access trojan named DeviceManager to Windows systems.
SOCRadar's Threat Research Unit says DOUBLECUP has operated since early June 2026, providing customers with licenses and a Go-based Windows tool for creating malicious campaigns and generating the code operators add to their websites.
The service handles much of the infrastructure required to conduct the attacks, including hosting the steganographic PNG images, managing session and signal endpoints, providing encryption keys, and automatically rebuilding payloads.
DOUBLECUP customers are responsible for creating and hosting the websites used to display the ClickFix prompts, adding the generated frontend code, and implementing any additional obfuscation or anti-analysis measures.
SOCRadar discovered DOUBLECUP while investigating an open directory at 213[.]139.77[.]109:9090 that contained test files. The same IP address was later identified as hosting the service's licensing panel.
To launch an attack, a DOUBLECUP customer uses the Go-based Windows application to configure the campaign's domain, URL path, steganography method, embed type, execution action, and payload locations.
This generates an API configuration endpoint that returns the steganographic image URL and file size, session endpoint, and commands customized for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, and Opera.
Operators then add DOUBLECUP's code to their ClickFix sites, which retrieves the configuration, preloads the steganographic image into the victim's browser cache, registers the session, selects the command matching the victim's browser, and copies it to the clipboard when the page is opened.
Malware hidden in the browser cache
In a new report, SOCRadar says it observed DOUBLECUP ClickFix campaigns using fake CAPTCHA prompts on login pages impersonating NetSuite, Odoo, HubSpot, and Salesforce, with the malicious code loaded through embedded iframes.
When a victim visits one of these sites, DOUBLECUP registers the session, determines the victim's public IP address, and forces the browser to download and cache a malicious PNG image.
The page then displays fake CAPTCHA-style instructions that attempt to convince visitors to paste and run a command automatically copied to their clipboard.
Once executed, the command searches the browser cache for the PNG based on its exact file size and uses the findstr or certutil commands to recover and execute the hidden first-stage payload inside the image.
The first payload launches a fileless second-stage dropper, which retrieves the victim's public IPv4 address and uses it to create a decryption key for the final encrypted payload.
After verifying the decrypted payload against a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, the dropper executes it in memory. SOCRadar says the final payloads are CountLoader and a new DeviceManager RAT.
2 malware payloads
SOCRadar identified two malware families delivered through DOUBLECUP, which are an updated version of CountLoader that targets Windows and macOS and what is believed to be a previously undocumented DeviceManager RAT.
CountLoader is used to harvest information about infected systems, checks for cryptocurrency wallet applications and browser extensions, determines whether Signal Desktop is installed, and establishes persistence through scheduled tasks.
CountLoader can also download and execute files, including MSI packages, PowerShell modules, and DLLs.
SOCRadar also recovered a macOS version compiled for Intel and Apple Silicon devices, which installs a LaunchAgent for persistence and uses built-in utilities such as curl, sw_vers, system_profiler, and ioreg to communicate with attacker-controlled servers.
DOUBLECUP was also seen delivering the DeviceManager malware, a modular Python-based Windows RAT that uses blockchain smart contracts to determine the IP address of its command-and-control server.
In countries not part of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), DeviceManager collects the machine GUID, disk identifier, user SID, hostname, username, operating system version, architecture, installed antivirus software, and domain information.
The malware uses a technique known as EtherHiding to retrieve its current C2 address from an Ethereum or Polygon smart contract, which makes it more resistant to disruption attempts.
The RAT uses DNS A and TXT records to steal system information, retrieve commands to execute, download payloads, and send command output back to the attackers.
This is not the first time ClickFix attacks have used steganography, as Huntress previously documented campaigns that concealed LummaC2 and Rhadamanthys payloads within the pixel data of PNG images.

articles.title: Los centros comerciales viven, la lucha sigue: un fondo inversor de Noruega ha comprado ocho grandes áreas en España
articles.text:
Sus siglas quizás no nos digan gran cosa en España, pero NBIM, el Norges Bank Investment Management, es un peso pesado de las finanzas mundiales. Gestiona el Fondo de Pensiones que rentabiliza la riqueza generada por el petróleo y gas de Noruega. Sus decisiones se miran con lupa, tanto por el dinero que maneja como por lo que revelan sobre el mercado. Y uno de sus últimos movimientos apunta a un sector que algunos analistas daban hace no tanto por condenado y ahora demuestra una vitalidad robusta: los centros comerciales de España.
De hecho el fondo noruego es el protagonista de un importante acuerdo comercial centrado en activos por valor de 1.500 millones de euros.
¿Qué ha pasado? La noticia la hizo pública el viernes Sierra Sonae, una compañía que se dedica entre otras cosas a la gestión de activos y administración de propiedades. Sus responsables han llegado a un alianza empresarial (para ser más precisos han formado una joint venture) con el poderoso Norges Bank para apostar por el negocio de los centros comerciales de la península ibérica.
En concreto, el objetivo de Sierra Sonae y el fondo noruego es adquirir una cartera de ocho instalaciones repartidas por España. En el sector se rumoreaba desde hace semanas que se estaba fraguando la operación, pero el acuerdo no se selló hasta hace unos días. Ahora debe recibir el aval de las autoridades.
¿Qué centros comerciales? Los activos que han despertado el apetito de NBIM y Sonae Sierra se reparten por tres regiones de España: la Comunidad de Madrid (Gran Plaza 2, Plaza Norte 2, Plaza Río 2, La Vaguada, Plaza Moraleja 2 y Plaza Loranca 2), Barcelona (Gran Vía 2) y Alicante (Plaza Mar 2).
No ha trascendido el importe exacto de la transacción, pero la propia Sierra Sonae se ha encargado de recordar dos cifras que dan una idea de su magnitud: la cartera que han adquirido tiene un valor bruto de alrededor de 1.500 millones de euros y suma una superficie bruta alquilable de más de 250.000 m2. A modo de referencia, en marzo la patronal del sector (AECC) estimaba que en España operan 592 centros que aglutinan una SBA de 16,9 millones de m2.
¿Se sabe algo más? Sí, algunos detalles extra. Sabemos que el acuerdo para adquirir esos centros comerciales ya está firmado, que sus promotores esperan ahora la 'bendición' de los reguladores e incluso la identidad del vendedor. Los activos formaban parte de la cartera de La Sociedad General Inmobiliaria de España (LSGI), firma especializada en operaciones inmobiliarias.
La joint venture impulsada por Sonae Sierra y NBIM deja abierta sin embargo la puerta para seguir explorando el sector. En el comunicado del viernes la primera avanza que, en el marco de la alianza con su socio noruego, se "evaluará de forma selectiva nuevas oportunidades en centros comerciales de la península ibérica que encajen con su perfil estratégico y de rentabilidad". Por lo pronto, sabemos que Sierra será la que asuma la gestión directa de la cartera recién comprada.
¿Se queda ahí? No. Los responsables de Sonae también han aprovechado para informar de que, "de forma independiente a esta alianza", ha decidido adquirir el 100% de SCCE. "Esta operación incluye la integración de un equipo de más de 130 profesionales que gestionan los ocho centros comerciales de la cartera adquirida, así como otros diez activos propiedad de terceros", aclara.
Tras ese movimiento dirigirá 73 centros comerciales en ocho países.
¿Por qué es importante? Primero, por el alcance de la operación en sí. No sabemos qué precio han acordado la joint venture y LSGI para el cambio de los ocho centros comerciales, pero sí que la cartera cuenta con un valor de 1.500 millones de euros. La segunda razón por la que la compra es interesante es porque confirma el interés inversor por los centros comerciales del país.
Además, en este caso concreto no hablamos de un agente invesor cualquiera: NBIM gestiona el Fondo Global de Pensiones del Gobierno de Noruega, creado en la década de 1990 para gestionar la riqueza generada por los recursos petroleros y de gas del país, actuando de reserva financiera y "pensando a largo plazo". Hoy se considera el mayor fondo soberano del planeta y de los más influyentes.
¿Cómo le va a los centros comerciales? No parece que les vaya mal. Al menos si nos fiamos de los datos de la AECC, que calcula que en 2025 las ventas del sector (incluye parques comerciales) crecieron un 6% y la afluencia un 2,4%, lo se que traduce en 1.995 millones de consumidores y 58.524 millones en ventas. La patronal registró además 32 operaciones de compraventa por valor de 2.000 millones y espera que de aquí a 2028 se pongan en marcha 36 proyectos.
No está mal si tenemos en cuenta que hace solo unos años se hablaba de un escenario muy diferente, una pérdida de competitividad general que, advertían algunos expertos, en última instancia derivaría en un "apocalipsis del retail".
La lógica era muy sencilla: ¿Quién iba a acudir a espacios masificados tras la pandemia? ¿Quién estaría interesado en comprar en centros pudiéndolo hacer online? ¿Para qué salir de casa e ir a grandes superficies si ya se podían ver películas prácticamente de estreno a buen precio en HBO o Netflix?
¿Solo apuesta el fondo noruego? Para nada. El sector leva ya tiempo haciendo gala de su dinamismo, con operaciones de compraventa que suman cientos de millones de euros y la puesta en marcha de nuevos complejos, lo que demuestra que hay inversores convencidos de que queda margen de crecimiento.
La clave de su éxito no está solo en mantener su tirón pese al cambio de tendencias y hábitos de consumo, sino en su capacidad para reinventarse explorando nuevos perfiles de negocio. En muchos casos su apuesta es ha sido clara (y exitosa): los centros comerciales ya no ofrecen solo mercancías o locales de hostelería, sino la posibilidad de "vivir experiencias" y crear recuerdos.

articles.title: Hécatombe chez Porsche : la marque de luxe sacrifie près d'un quart de ses salariés
articles.text:
Personne ne semble épargné par la crise, pas même les marques qui revendiquaient historiquement une rentabilité extraordinaire. C’est le cas de Porsche, qui subit de plein fouet les complications du marché. Pour limiter la casse, la solution la plus simple est cruelle mais évidente : supprimer des emplois. La marque allemande, qui avait déjà annoncé 4 400 postes en moins, poursuit donc de plus belle.
Un plan social choc qui fait vaciller un géant du luxe
Dans le cadre d’un plan de restructuration négocié entre la direction et les syndicats représentant le personnel, 5 000 emplois passeront ainsi à la trappe d’ici 2035. Ce nouveau paquet s’ajoute alors aux 3 900 suppressions initialement annoncées en février 2025 et aux 500 autres déjà indiquées par Michael Leiters, le PDG de la marque. Le nombre de licenciements passe donc au total à 9 400.
Près d’un quart des effectifs sacrifiés : la saignée continue
Il y a ainsi de la casse, même si Porsche précise que ces réductions sont « socialement responsables ». Rappelons que le constructeur allemand employait près de 43 000 personnes fin 2024. C’est ainsi presque le quart de la masse salariale qui quittera l’entreprise. Les raisons d’un tel effondrement sont connues : la situation de Porsche sur le marché chinois, autrefois très porteur, s’est considérablement durcie.
La Chine et l’électrique : le double séisme qui plonge Porsche dans la crise
Plusieurs mesures d’économies sont bien sûr possibles, mais selon Daniel Schwarz, analyste automobile pour la banque d’investissement Metzler, les suppressions d’emplois « sont inévitables pour réduire les coûts, car un retour à une forte croissance en Chine n’est plus d’actualité ». D’autres marques premium allemandes comme BMW et Mercedes taillent aussi sévèrement dans les effectifs pour tenter d’amortir leur chute.
Ces constructeurs ont un point commun : ils ont massivement investi dans l’électrique pour finalement se rendre compte que les clients ne suivent pas. Ce véritable trou dans la poche a logiquement fragilisé leurs finances sans garantir un retour sur investissement. Porsche ajoute tout de même que l’accord passé avec les syndicats comprend aussi des garanties pour maintenir la production dans les usines pendant cinq années supplémentaires.
Des milliards investis pour tenter de sauver les meubles
D’autre part, 2,1 milliards d’euros vont être investis dans l’usine principale de Porsche à Stuttgart et au centre de recherche et développement à Weissach. Mieux que rien, même si cela ne suffira pas à atténuer les inquiétudes. Il faut dire qu’Oliver Blume, le PDG du groupe Volkswagen, estime qu’il faut atteindre à minima 100 000 licenciements pour rester dans la course face aux constructeurs chinois.

articles.title: Visa to Acquire Fraud Intelligence Firm BioCatch for $2.4 Billion
articles.text:
Visa has agreed to acquire fraud prevention company BioCatch for $2.4 billion in cash as the payments giant looks to expand its cybersecurity and financial crime detection capabilities.
Founded in 2011, BioCatch provides behavioral biometrics technology that analyzes application, device, network and user activity to distinguish legitimate customers from fraudsters in real time.
Its artificial intelligence and machine learning models examine thousands of signals, including keystrokes, mouse activity, touchscreen gestures, device handling and signs that a user may be acting under coercion. The technology is designed to identify account takeovers, scams, money mule activity, application fraud and other financial crimes before a transaction is completed.
BioCatch says its technology analyzes 19 billion online banking sessions each month and protects 760 million users across 1.8 billion devices. The company serves more than 350 financial institutions in 21 countries, including over 100 of the world’s largest banks.
“BioCatch will help our clients stop fraud before it reaches the point of payment,” said Andrew Torre, president of value-added services at Visa. “This acquisition is part of our strategy to help clients prevent cyber threats upstream, building trust into every transaction.”
The acquisition will add BioCatch’s behavioral and device intelligence to Visa’s existing portfolio of cyber, fraud, risk and security products. Visa said it has invested more than $13 billion in technology and infrastructure over the past five years to protect the payments ecosystem.
Permira initially invested in BioCatch in 2023 and acquired a majority stake the following year in a transaction that valued the company at $1.3 billion.
The deal is part of a broader push by major payment companies to expand beyond transaction processing into cybersecurity and fraud intelligence. Mastercard completed its $2.65 billion acquisition of threat intelligence firm Recorded Future in 2024, while Visa acquired fraud prevention company Featurespace that same year.
BioCatch is being acquired from funds advised by private equity firm Permira and other shareholders. The transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions and is expected to close by the end of Visa’s fiscal second quarter of 2027.
